lecture_metadata.title: Lecture 1: Probabilities
lecture_metadata.main_purpose: Introduce statistics as model-mediated reasoning from finite, imperfect measurements to claims about reality, then motivate probability distributions and descriptive parameters as tools for representing uncertainty.

central_arc: Statistics is needed because reality is hidden from direct view; we only get measurements and must reason through models.
Data are finite measurement products, often heavily processed, so what counts as data already depends on collection and transformation choices.
Before modeling, students must separate different kinds of data quality problems and understand that some failures come from collection rather than from later analysis.
Probability enters as the language for uncertainty, and the lecture sharply separated randomness in the world from uncertainty due to incomplete knowledge.
Probability distributions and their parameters are not just formulas: their plots, code, and summaries must be interpreted as claims about likely values, spread, asymmetry, and tails.

sections.section_title: Why statistics exists / What is statistics
sections.teaching_goal: Help students see statistics as indirect reasoning about hidden reality through data and models rather than as a machine for extracting truth directly.
orally_sharpened_distinctions: Reality is what we care about, data are the measurements we can see, and models are the ideas that let measurements say something about reality.
Statistics tells us what the data imply about a model, not what reality is with certainty.
The same measurements can be compatible with more than one model.
resolved_confusions: Why statistics is still useful even though we never 'see inside the box': it constrains ideas about reality rather than revealing reality directly.
Why the reality-data-model relation is iterative: data update models, and models generate new questions and new data collection.
warnings_common_mistakes: Do not talk as if statistical analysis directly reveals the true state of the world.
Do not treat agreement between data and a model as proof that the model is true.

oral_interpretations.takeaway: The figures were used to show that measurements only become informative after being interpreted through a model, and that inference always stays one step removed from reality.

high_value_checks: Can the student explain the role of the model in the reality-data-model diagram?
Can the student explain why statistics can inform a model without guaranteeing truth?
Can the student describe the loop from data to model revision to further data collection?
incidental_or_do_not_assess: Historical names and dates used for motivation.
The scientist-versus-engineer framing used as general motivation.

sections.teaching_goal: Make students understand data as finite observations produced by measurement processes, including preprocessing and derived quantities.
orally_sharpened_distinctions: Data are not reality itself; they are recorded outputs of a measurement process.
A derived or normalized quantity can still be data if it is part of the measurement-and-processing pipeline.
A dataset is finite at the moment of analysis even if more data could be collected later.
resolved_confusions: Why an apparently obvious claim like 'data are finite' matters later: students will be tempted to reason as if more data were already available.
Why preprocessing does not make a quantity cease to be data.
warnings_common_mistakes: Do not ignore the chain of operations that produced a number and then speak as if it were raw reality.
Do not slide from 'I could collect more data' to 'my current dataset is effectively unlimited.'

oral_interpretations.item: Raw versus normalized cerebellar volume example
oral_interpretations.takeaway: The example showed that a transformed quantity may be more useful than a raw one because it better matches the scientific comparison of interest.

high_value_checks: Can the student explain why normalized cerebellar volume may be a better measure than raw cerebellar volume for some questions?
Can the student explain why a processed quantity can still count as data?
Can the student state why finiteness of the dataset matters for later inference?
incidental_or_do_not_assess: Detailed MRI physics or voxel-processing specifics.

sections.teaching_goal: Teach students to distinguish major sources of data imperfection and to recognize where interpretation breaks before formal statistics even begins.
orally_sharpened_distinctions: Precision is consistency of repeated measurement; validity is whether the measure tracks the intended thing; reliability is whether the same process or rater gives stable answers.
Missing data can actively bias conclusions, not just make them noisier.
A proxy measure is something observed in place of the quantity actually of interest.
resolved_confusions: Validity was made more concrete as requiring a meaningful monotonic relation between the measure and the thing cared about.
Reliability was distinguished from mere imprecision by examples where the procedure is stable or unstable across raters or times.
Proxy measures were clarified as often unavoidable rather than automatically illegitimate.
warnings_common_mistakes: Do not assume statistics can rescue fundamentally bad data collection.
Do not talk as if a proxy measure is identical to the target construct.
Do not treat ethical issues as separate from data quality and use.

oral_interpretations.takeaway: Sampling bias can create systematic failure in real devices even when the measurement technology seems established.
Measurement error can have harmful consequences when people act on a noisy signal as if it were accurate enough for control.
Extracellular recordings and calcium signals were used to show how scientific inference often depends on imperfect stand-ins for the variable of interest.

high_value_checks: Can the student distinguish precision, validity, and reliability on a new example?
Can the student explain why missing data may reverse or distort a conclusion rather than merely widen uncertainty?
Can the student explain what makes a measure a proxy and what inferential caution that creates?
incidental_or_do_not_assess: Specific historical or policy details of the economics spreadsheet example.
Detailed ethics checklist language beyond the core ideas of consent, privacy, power asymmetry, and downstream harm.

sections.teaching_goal: Help students recognize common data types while seeing that type treatment can sometimes be an analytic choice rather than a fixed property.
orally_sharpened_distinctions: Continuous, ordinal, and categorical are the main working types in the lecture.
The ontological type of a variable and the way an analyst chooses to treat it are related but not always identical.
resolved_confusions: An ordinal scale with many levels can sometimes be treated as continuous for convenience, provided that the choice is recognized as a modeling decision.
Real datasets often combine several types simultaneously.
warnings_common_mistakes: Do not treat recoding or type simplification as a trivial move with no consequences.
Do not assume every variable comes with a single uniquely forced analysis type.

oral_interpretations.takeaway: The variable list was used to show that one dataset can contain categorical, ordinal, and continuous measurements together, with some borderline choices handled pragmatically.

high_value_checks: Can the student classify example variables and explain any borderline choice?
Can the student explain why treating an ordinal variable as continuous can be acceptable in some contexts?
Can the student connect data type recognition to later model choice?
incidental_or_do_not_assess: The exact list of sample variables from the cerebellar table.

sections.teaching_goal: Establish probability as the language for uncertainty and sharply separate aleatory uncertainty from epistemic uncertainty.
orally_sharpened_distinctions: Aleatory uncertainty is uncertainty because the process itself is stochastic.
Epistemic uncertainty is uncertainty because relevant information is missing, hidden, or unevenly distributed.
Repeated-trial frequency is a natural interpretation for aleatory cases but not for one-off predictive situations like wars or markets.
resolved_confusions: Why different people can legitimately assign different probabilities in epistemic settings: they condition on different information.
Why both types of uncertainty can coexist in scientific data: some variation comes from the world, some from limited knowledge and measurement.
warnings_common_mistakes: Do not collapse every use of probability into long-run frequency language.
Do not describe single-case prediction-market probabilities as if they referred to repeated identical worlds.
Do not over-read the brief frequentist-versus-Bayesian preview in this lecture as a complete treatment.

oral_interpretations.takeaway: The coin-flip plot illustrated the frequentist long-run convergence idea tied to aleatory uncertainty.
These examples were used to show epistemic probability as a graded state of knowledge that changes with information rather than with repeated trials.

high_value_checks: Can the student explain the roulette-versus-poker contrast in terms of aleatory and epistemic uncertainty?
Can the student explain why more information changes epistemic uncertainty but does not remove aleatory uncertainty from a stochastic process?
Can the student connect the two uncertainty types to the data-model loop used in the lecture?
incidental_or_do_not_assess: Specific Polymarket prices, dates, or war-specific details.
The brief value judgment about Bayesian versus frequentist statistics.

sections.teaching_goal: Teach students to interpret probability distributions as model objects over possible values, including the difference between discrete probabilities, continuous densities, and cumulative probability.
orally_sharpened_distinctions: For discrete random variables, values get probabilities; for continuous random variables, values get densities and probability lives over intervals.
A PDF describes local density; a CDF gives accumulated probability up to a point.
Samples drawn from a distribution are data generated by that distribution, not the same thing as the distribution itself.
resolved_confusions: Why the probability between two continuous values is obtained by subtracting CDF values or integrating the density over the interval.
Why the top-row versus bottom-row plots in the PDF/CDF comparison are different kinds of objects.
warnings_common_mistakes: Do not read the height of a continuous PDF at a single point as a point probability.
Do not confuse a simulated histogram with the underlying distribution that generated it.

oral_interpretations.item: Sampling from a binomial distribution and comparing histogram to the PMF
oral_interpretations.takeaway: The notebook demonstration linked abstract distributions to generated datasets while preserving the distinction between model and sample.

oral_interpretations.item: Normal distribution with shaded region from -2 to 0
oral_interpretations.takeaway: The shaded region was explicitly interpreted as interval probability computed from CDF(0) minus CDF(-2).
The code was used mainly to reinforce the meaning of the objects: draw the density, accumulate it, and use the CDF to get probabilities over ranges.

high_value_checks: Can the student explain the discrete-versus-continuous distinction without saying that a continuous point has a regular probability?
Can the student explain how to compute probability between two continuous values from the CDF?
Can the student explain what the PDF/CDF comparison plots are showing?
incidental_or_do_not_assess: Package-specific function names unless they are needed to interpret the notebook output.

sections.teaching_goal: Show how a distribution can be summarized compactly, while making clear that different descriptive numbers capture different aspects of shape.
orally_sharpened_distinctions: Parameters are convenient compact descriptors of a distribution; descriptive summaries like center and spread are another compact language for the same object.
Mean, median, and mode are different notions of the 'middle,' and they separate when the distribution is asymmetric.
Kurtosis is about tails relative to peak and relative to the normal baseline, not simply about having a larger standard deviation.
resolved_confusions: The median was tied directly to the CDF as the point where cumulative probability reaches 0.5.
The mean was clarified as tail-sensitive and therefore pulled toward the long tail in an asymmetric distribution.
The repeated student question on kurtosis was resolved by showing how same-standard-deviation distributions can still differ in tail weight and by explaining why excess kurtosis subtracts 3.
warnings_common_mistakes: Do not assume a single number can fully describe a distribution.
Do not treat wider tails as automatically the same concept as greater spread.
Do not memorize kurtosis as a formula without understanding the comparison to the normal distribution.

oral_interpretations.item: Asymmetric gamma distribution with mean, median, and mode marked
oral_interpretations.takeaway: The plot was used to show that these summaries coincide only in special symmetric cases and separate in skewed distributions.
The slide framed two-number description as center plus typical distance from center.
The panels were interpreted qualitatively: skewness tracks tail direction, and kurtosis tracks how quickly the tails die out relative to a normal distribution with the same spread.

high_value_checks: Can the student explain where mean, median, and mode sit in an asymmetric distribution and why?
Can the student explain why two distributions can share a standard deviation yet differ in kurtosis?
Can the student interpret the sign of skewness from the direction of the long tail?
incidental_or_do_not_assess: Deriving the third- and fourth-moment formulas in detail.
Exact Greek-letter notation for every parameter.

highest_value_distinctions: Density over a range vs point probability for continuous distributions.
sound_right_but_wrong_risks: Saying that statistics or a fitted model directly reveals reality.
Treating bad collection or proxy problems as if later statistics alone can fix them.
Using long-run frequency language for one-off epistemic predictions.
Equating heavier tails with merely having a larger standard deviation.
important_interpretations: Normalized cerebellar volume as an example of processed data that may be better aligned with the scientific target.
Running proportion of heads as the lecture's concrete image of long-run aleatory probability.
CDF difference as the way to read interval probability from a continuous distribution.
Gamma / skewness / kurtosis plots as evidence that different summary numbers answer different descriptive questions.
brief_or_incidental_topics: Historical survey of early statistics figures.
Detailed prediction-market mechanics and payout arithmetic.
Exact moment-formula details beyond conceptual interpretation.

static_materials_sufficient_for: Basic named definitions of data types and of terms like probability distribution, random variable, and parameter.
The broad lecture flow from measurement to data to probabilistic models.
The existence of common summary measures such as mean, median, mode, variance, and standard deviation.
minutes_matter_most_for: Treating the reality-data-model diagram as a claim about indirect inference rather than as decorative lecture framing.
Remembering that data are finite and may be heavily processed while still counting as data.
Separating precision, validity, reliability, proxy measurement, and missing-data problems in conceptually usable ways.
Interpreting aleatory versus epistemic uncertainty, PDF versus CDF, and kurtosis versus spread in the way the lecture actually taught them.
do_not_turn_into_direct_questions: Do not ask students to recall historical names, dates, or book titles from the motivational slides.
Do not ask for Polymarket-specific facts, exact prices, or war-specific details from the example.
Do not turn package syntax or notebook library names into standalone assessment targets.
Do not make the brief frequentist-versus-Bayesian preview in this lecture carry more assessment weight than the lecture itself gave it.
